transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08 
Start time: 15:00 UTC 
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood CSM); Dr. Lillian Park, Arjun Mehta, Samira Ortiz, Ravi Shen (Sable)

Summary: quick kickoff to align on quality evaluation rubric for the pilot, define golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination/format checks, scoring weights, workload sizing and timeline for a 3-week pilot. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics covered: intro & goals; success criteria; golden prompts; regression suite; hallucination detection; format/structure checks; scoring approach; workload sizing & perf benchmarks; timeline and logistics; security questions; next steps.

[00:00:12] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro, im maya patel, AE for redwood, and with me is ethan li, our solutions engineer.
[00:00:24] Arjun: thanks maya, arjun here, CTO at sable. we have lillian and samira as well. goal for today is to lock down what success looks like for the pilot — particularly on quality — and the practical bits like load and timeline.
[00:00:39] Ethan: perfect, we'll try to be concrete. first, what does success look like from your side? is it accuracy, low hallucination, format fidelity, or something else?
[00:00:53] Dr. Lillian: for us it's a combination. top priority: zero critical hallucinations on patient directives, second is consistent structured outputs that map to our EMR schema, and third is latency - sub 800ms p95 end-to-end for the interactive clinician flow — though cost is also a constraint.
[00:01:17] Samira: to add, we want a regression baseline so we can detect model drift when we swap model variants or quantization.
[00:01:26] Ethan: great, that maps well to a quality rubric: hallucination tolerance, format compliance, semantic correctness, and latency/cost buckets. we usually recommend a weighted scoring where hallucination is high weight for medtech.
[00:01:42] Ravi: can you expand on what counts as a hallucination in the rubric? small inferred details vs. inventing procedures?
[00:01:51] Maya: good q. we'll propose categories: critical hallucination (invented diagnosis/procedure that could change care), moderate (plausible but unverified assertions), and minor (stylistic or non-actionable). criticals are immediate fail.
[00:02:06] Arjun: ok that makes sense. what about format checks — our EMR schema is strict, so we need field-level validation and type checks.
[00:02:15] Ethan: we can add automated validators in the regression harness: schema conformance, field presence, value ranges, and canonicalization. we'll flag partial parses. sometimes tokenization leads to weird punctuation causing JSON parse errors — we've seen that.
[00:02:34] Samira: how do you measure hallucination rates programmatically? do you use model-based detectors or human annotation?
[00:02:41] Ethan: a mix. for the pilot we recommend manual annotation for the golden set and spot checks, plus automated heuristics: NER overlap, contradiction detection, and confidence calibration. for production, teams often add a lightweight model-based filter.
[00:02:58] Maya: we typically create a golden prompts set — 50 to 150 prompts — that cover critical paths. each prompt has expected outputs and acceptance criteria. those become the regression suite.
[00:03:12] Dr. Lillian: our critical path is clinical-note-summarization and discharge instruction generation; can you adapt prompts for those?
[00:03:20] Ethan: absolutely. example golden prompt: 'Summarize the encounter and extract discharge instructions as a JSON with keys: diagnosis, medications, followUpDays, criticalAlerts'. we'll provide anchor outputs and edge cases — e.g., multi-comorbidity, conflicting notes.
[00:03:38] Ravi: we also need hallucination checks for cited references. sometimes clinicians want papers or guideline refs included; we prefer the assistant to cite only exact matches from our internal knowledge base.
[00:03:49] Maya: we'll include citation rules in the rubric: 'If not directly verifiable in supplied KB, respond "no citation available" rather than fabricating.' that's a hard fail for us.
[00:04:00] Arjun: ok, moving to scoring: how do you propose weights?
[00:04:06] Ethan: recommended default: 40% hallucination (critical weighted heavily), 25% format/schema compliance, 20% semantic correctness (F1/ROUGE-ish over key fields), 15% latency/cost bucket. We can tune numbers with you.
[00:04:23] Samira: semantics scoring — do you compute exact match on fields or use similarity? example: 'aspirin 81mg' vs '81 mg aspirin' should be equivalent.
[00:04:34] Ethan: we use normalized exact matches for structured fields (normalize units and naming), and semantic similarity for free-text summaries (embedding similarity plus human spot checks).
[00:04:46] Maya: and for thresholds, we usually propose pass/fail gates: no critical hallucinations in golden set, >=95% schema conformance, semantic score >=0.85 on summary tasks, and p95 latency <=800ms for interactive. those are negotiable.
[00:05:02] Dr. Lillian: sensible. what about sample sizes for statistical significance?
[00:05:08] Ethan: for hallucination you want enough samples to detect a 2-3% difference with confidence. practical pilot: 200-500 examples across prompts with stratified edge cases. for structure conformance, 200 should be fine.
[00:05:23] Arjun: that aligns with our ability to share 300 de-identified records. we need to confirm de-id approach; security team will vet.
[00:05:31] Maya: noted, we'll wait for Samira's 100 samples first and then scale.
[00:05:36] Ravi: workload sizing — what inputs do you need to size the pilot infra? token distribution, concurrency, avg doc length?
[00:05:45] Ethan: yes. practical ask: sample avg tokens per prompt, avg response tokens, expected concurrent sessions (clinicians using tool at same time), and daily throughput. start with worst-case interactive load — e.g., 50 concurrent users with 1 request every 30s — that translates to x tokens/sec.
[00:06:00] Samira: our average note is ~800 tokens, summary output ~120 tokens. concurrent interactive users during rounds maybe 30-50. backlog batch jobs (nightly summarization) run on 2000 notes per hour.
[00:06:12] Ethan: great — for the pilot we can spin up a dedicated job runner for batch and a low-latency instance for interactive. we'll give you recommended instance sizes and token/sec throughput for each model variant we test.
[00:06:24] Maya: on models — are you open to testing both hosted redwood and a private deployment?
[00:06:29] Arjun: security prefers private or VPC. we need to evaluate both for cost comparison; but pilot may start as hosted with PII redaction and then move to private.
[00:06:38] Ethan: that's common. for private we need IP allowlist and VPC peering info. we'll send a network diagram and required ports.
[00:06:47] Samira: what about quantization/throughput tradeoffs? our accuracy bar is high.
[00:06:52] Ethan: we'll include model variants: fp16 baseline, int8 quantized, and a CPU-optimized quantized path if you want on-prem. each will be scored in the rubric for quality and performance. we expect small semantic drops with aggressive quantization on some models; that's why regression is critical.
[00:07:08] Dr. Lillian: can we automate regression gating so that any model swap fails if hallucination increases beyond X?
[00:07:14] Ethan: yes, in the rollout we support canary checks and automatic rollback if quality metrics degrade. Redwood Console will show token-level cost, p95 latency, and regression diffs.
[00:07:24] Ravi: benchmarks — what concrete tests will you run?
[00:07:28] Ethan: two sets: quality bench (golden prompts, human labels) and perf bench (synthetic load with realistic token distributions). quality bench is run at baseline and after model changes. perf bench measures throughput, p50/p95 latency, and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:07:43] Maya: we'll propose a pilot sequence: week 0 (setup, data ingest, golden prompt selection), week 1 (baseline quality + small perf run), week 2 (quantized variants + regression run), week 3 (final eval & handoff). overall 3-week pilot.
[00:07:57] Arjun: timeline OK, though our compliance review may add a week. can that be parallelized?
[00:08:03] Jordan (CSM): yes we can run non-PII synthetic benchmarks while compliance is finishing. that will get perf numbers early.
[00:08:10] Samira: about annotation cost — who annotates the golden set?
[00:08:14] Maya: we can help with annotation tooling and initial labeling for a fee; many customers do a mix. for the pilot Redwood will do the initial scoring for the golden set to bootstrap.
[00:08:24] Dr. Lillian: good to know. security checklist: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, audit logs — can you share docs?
[00:08:31] Maya: yes. action: we'll send SOC 2 summary, network diagram, and KMS integration notes.
[00:08:37] Arjun: do you support customer-managed keys in private?
[00:08:40] Ethan: yes, for private deployments and some dedicated options. we'll outline options.
[00:08:45] Ravi: any gotchas around PII redaction?
[00:08:48] Ethan: redaction needs to be done pre-send or with a deterministic pipeline; otherwise model can memorize. we'll suggest a pre-processing redaction step as part of the harness.
[00:08:57] Samira: ok, practicalities — share your eval spreadsheet and sample prompts and we'll iterate.
[00:09:02] Maya: absolutely, we'll share golden prompt template and scoring sheet by Friday.
[00:09:06] Arjun: who will run the perf tests from your side?
[00:09:09] Ethan: we'll run perf tests with your network configs, but you'll be able to reproduce — we provide the harness and scripts.
[00:09:15] Dr. Lillian: what's your recommendation for pass/fail on cost? we have strict budget constraints.
[00:09:21] Maya: for pilots we separate cost from quality gating: quality gates first, then we present cost tradeoffs and optimization suggestions (batching, caching KV, model variant). if cost is beyond your threshold we'll propose autoscaling and caching strategies to reduce unit cost.
[00:09:36] Ravi: please include an estimated cost-per-1000-tokens for each variant in the report.
[00:09:40] Ethan: yes, perf run will produce cost estimates and suggestions from Redwood Optimize module.
[00:09:45] Samira: any other competitors we should be benchmarking against?
[00:09:48] Maya: customers often benchmark against hosted Anthropic/OpenAI and self-hosted Llama stacks. we can include a lightweight comparison if you want.
[00:09:58] Arjun: let's include OpenAI for quality baseline only (not for perf).
[00:10:02] Ethan: noted.
[00:10:06] Maya: wrapping to logistics — recap of owners and due dates. action items on the doc.
[00:10:12] Jordan: i'll own scheduling the baseline run once data is in.
[00:10:16] Samira: we will aim to send the first 100 de-identified cases by Monday.
[00:10:20] Maya: great. any final Qs?
[00:10:23] Arjun: one last: what kind of reporting format do you provide? csv, dashboard, and a concise one-pager?
[00:10:29] Ethan: we'll deliver a dashboard (Redwood Console), exportable CSVs of per-example scores, and an executive one-pager with pass/fail and recommendations.
[00:10:39] Dr. Lillian: thanks. sounds good.
[00:10:41] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security packet.
[00:10:45] Arjun: thanks all.
[00:10:48] [meeting ends but call remains for final 37 minutes of live Q&A between Ethan and Samira about implementation details — transcript continues with technical back-and-forth]
[00:11:10] Samira: on the harness, can it validate nested JSON fields? our schema has arrays of meds and each med needs dose/unit fields.
[00:11:20] Ethan: yes, it supports nested validation; we run canonicalization and unit normalization; we'll include unit tests for edge cases.
[00:11:34] Samira: for the embedding similarity checks, what threshold do you recommend for semantic pass?
[00:11:40] Ethan: for summary-level embeddings we start at 0.8 cosine for pass and review anything 0.7-0.8 manually.
[00:11:49] Samira: ok. and for human annotation, do you support a UI?
[00:11:52] Ethan: we have a lightweight reviewer UI and CSV back-and-forth; initial pilot we'll use the UI for labels to speed iteration.
[00:12:02] Samira: about token accounting — does redwood show token usage per-request in logs?
[00:12:06] Jordan: yes, token-level breakdown, per-route cost and latency, and per-request KV cache hits if configured.
[00:12:14] Samira: good. for model swapping, do you do warm cache priming?
[00:12:18] Ethan: yes, we do proactive priming and continuous batching to reduce p95 spikes after a rollout.
[00:12:25] Samira: any known failure modes when running large batch summarization overnight?
[00:12:29] Ethan: tail latencies and memory pressure on KV cache if sequences are much longer than expected; we define batch size heuristics and guardrails.
[00:12:37] Samira: perfect — thanks.
[00:12:40] [rest of the call is logistics and re-iterating action items; timestamps skip forward]
[00:25:00] Maya: reiterate deliverables: golden prompts + scoring sheet (Redwood), sample data (Sable), perf harness (Redwood), net & compliance docs (Redwood), schedule baseline run (Jordan).
[00:25:20] Arjun: noted. thanks.
[00:25:30] Maya: we'll aim to have the first draft rubric by 2026-04-10 and a kickoff for the baseline run week of 2026-04-20.
[00:25:40] Samira: sounds good.
[00:25:45] Maya: thanks everyone — end call.
